https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/videos/c171nn.text: What triggered the mass migrant crossings into Ceuta? What triggered the mass migrant crossings into Ceuta? Close Over the last 24 hours, the tiny Spanish territory of Ceuta - home to around 83,000 people - has seen an unprecedented surge in migrant arrivals. An estimated 60,000 people from Morocco are believed to have crossed into the North African enclave that has long been a focal point for migrant attempting to reach Europe. Dozens of people died while trying to make the crossing. On Friday evening, Spanish officials confirmed that more than 48,000 of the migrants had voluntarily returned to Morocco. BBC's Sarah Rainsford explains what may have triggered the surge in crossings and what happens next. https://www.aol.co.uk/articles/massive-u.text: Dan Sabbagh in Kyiv Updated Sun, August 16, 2026 at 4:10 PM UTC 2 Ukraine has launched one of its largest drone attacks since the start of the war, causing a fire at a distribution warehouse near Moscow and killing at least six people overnight, according to Russian authorities. The defence ministry in Moscow said it had shot down 1,478 Ukrainian drones in the past 24 hours – the highest ever total claimed – in an escalating air war in which seven Ukrainians were also killed as Russia bombed 13 locations inside the country. A huge fire engulfed a 250,000 sq metre building near Podolsk, 25 miles south of Moscow’s city centre, belonging to the Wildberries distribution company. The facility was disabled as a result, Ukraine’s military said. Sergei Sobyanin, the mayor of Moscow, said 600 drones targeted the Moscow region overnight, of which 201 were destroyed. One person was reported killed in the region, while Ukraine said a second warehouse at nearby Domodedovo was also targeted. Interactive The Russian news agency RIA Novosti reported that the figure was the largest daily total claimed by the defence ministry, exceeding a record that had been set only the day before, though the figure is probably exaggerated and could not be verified. Experts said Russian numbers needed to be treated with caution but added that the scale of damage caused overnight nevertheless demonstrated how rapidly Ukraine had expanded its long-range attack capabilities in 2026. Serhii Kuzan, the chair of the Ukrainian Security and Cooperation Center, a thinktank, said Russian authorities “deliberately inflate their figures” to make exaggerated claims about the effectiveness of their air defence. But he said that “against the backdrop of increased production of Ukrainian long-range drones and missiles, both the number of strikes and the scale of Ukrainian weaponry’s deployment are on the rise” as the war continues. Kuzan argued that it was “quite possible” it was the largest-scale attack on the Moscow region, and it was “at least on a par” with the May strikes on an oil refinery in the Kapotnya area near Moscow. A rapid development of largely homegrown technologies, including the Flamingo cruise missile and the FP-1 long-range fixed-wing drone from Fire Point, have allowed Ukraine to bomb warehouses, oil refineries, ports and military facilities up to 1,500 miles from its border. Related: Ukraine war briefing: Kyiv faces missile barrage after Zelenskyy targets Russian satellite network Ukraine can now almost match the deep-strike capability that Russia has had since the beginning of the war using large drones and cruise missiles, though it still does not possess the high-speed ballistic missiles fired frequently by Moscow. At the same time, both sides’ air defences are stretched to the point of near exhaustion, leading to a rise in civilian casualties and worries that the impact of the conflict beyond the immediate frontlines will only increase into the winter. Kuzan said: “With every successful strike, Russia’s economic and military capabilities are diminished, and the Kremlin faces a new dilemma: how to counter this in a war of attrition.” In the past month, Kyiv has shifted focus to attacking facilities linked to Wildberries, used widely by businesses to support online retail. Ukraine says the warehouses are used by the military for logistics, though they also store stock sold by large and small Russian businesses. Ukraine’s military said on Sunday it had disabled seven out of 10 of the company’s largest warehouses in an effort to hurt the Russian economy and affect ordinary citizens financially, in a strike conducted with FP-1 drones. Five people were reported to have been killed in Russia’s southern Rostov region, which borders Ukraine, and the local governor said a further 150 incoming drones had been destroyed. Ukraine said it had targeted a factory that produced rocket fuel in Kamensk-Shakhtinsky, causing a fire there. Russian drone and missile attacks killed two people in the central city of Kryvyi Rih, while a Spanish F-18 jet shot down what appeared to be a Russia drone that had crossed over the border into Romania. The Spanish fighter was part of a Nato patrol mission and shot down the drone at about 5am after it crossed into Romanian airspace. “The drone appears to be Russian,” a Nato military spokesperson said. Andrey Vorobyov, the governor of the Moscow region, said the assault on the region was “one of the most massive drone attacks in recent memory”. Video footage on social media showed a fast fire raging across the Wildberries warehouse complex. Russian attacks on Ukraine also killed two in the Sumy border region and three others across the country. A ballistic missile attack on Kyiv shortly before 3am injured six and caused several fires in the capital. A blaze caused by the attacks destroyed a large part of the Petrovka book market in the Obolonskyi district in Kyiv overnight, with some booksellers reporting they had lost their entire stock in the incident. “There is nothing. Nobody has anything left,” said Natalya, a bookstore owner who was interviewed by Ukraine’s Hromadske website. “Everything burned down. I was selling foreign language [textbooks] for schoolchildren. We were waiting for September so that everyone would have textbooks … But what happened happened.” Ukraine’s president, Volodymyr Zelenskyy, praised the work of the country’s emergency services and accused the Russians of attacking ordinary people. “Wherever the Russians can reach with their ballistic missiles, they strike civilian infrastructure,” he said in a social media post. Zelenskyy said Russia had launched more than 1,550 attack drones, nearly 1,560 guided aerial bombs and 62 missiles at Ukrainian cities and communities over the past week, most of them ballistic missiles of various types. Though Ukraine is effective at stopping slower-moving drones, it has little to no defence against high-speed ballistics, its stock of US-made Patriot interceptor missiles – the only weapons capable of knocking them out – having been run down. Jaishankar India remains in continuous contact with both Ukraine and Russia as it seeks ways to help end the ongoing conflict. External Affairs Minister S. Jaishankar said India is exploring ideas and suggestions that could contribute to reducing tensions and supporting efforts toward a peaceful resolution. India is maintaining direct and continuous communication with both Ukraine and Russia as it explores possible ways to help reduce tensions and eventually bring the ongoing conflict to an end, External Affairs Minister S. Jaishankar says in Warsaw. His remarks came shortly after his visit to Kyiv, where he held talks with Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy and Ukrainian Foreign Minister Andrii Sybiha , underlining New Delhi’s continued effort to remain engaged with both sides of the war. https://dominicanrepublicpost.com/romani.text: World News Romania says Russia-run sabotage network set fire near weapons factory 26 October 2026 Support us This content originally appeared on Al Jazeera . Romanian authorities say they have uncovered a network “coordinated” by Russia that they believe was responsible for a fire at an industrial site near a state-owned weapons factory in September. Romania’s Intelligence Service said on Monday that the blaze in the central city of Brasov on September 14 was “part of a wider campaign of sabotage operations coordinated” by Russia amid its full-scale invasion of Ukraine. list of 3 items list 1 of 3 Ukraine says Russian drone attack sinks ship in Romanian waters list 2 of 3 ‘Block, blunt, break’: What’s in NATO’s new Russia war plan? list 3 of 3 Seven missing after two tankers catch fire off Romania’s Black Sea coast end of list The agency said the operations were aimed at arms manufacturers and “other targets of military and industrial interest”. “These actions are intended to intimidate, undermine defence capabilities and weaken the contribution of the targeted states to European and regional security,” it said in a statement. There was no immediate comment from Russia on Romania’s claim. Moscow has previously repeatedly denied such accusations. Romania’s Directorate for Investigating Organized Crime and Terrorism, known as DIICOT, said three people had been involved in the Brasov fire – two Belarusians and a Ukrainian, all living in European Union countries. Two were “tracked down and remanded in custody in Germany while they were preparing to commit similar offenses”, the directorate said. The third remains at large in Poland. According to Romania’s Intelligence Service, recruits for such networks are often found on social media and are first offered money “for a seemingly harmless task”, such as “observing or photographing certain targets”. Over time, “the tasks become increasingly serious, potentially involving acts of vandalism, arson or even murder”, it said. Advertisement Romania, a member of the EU and NATO, shares a border of more than 600km with Ukraine. Its centrist president, Nicusor Dan, has said the country is a target of a hybrid war that Russia is waging to destabilise nations backing Kyiv, citing drone incursions into Romanian airspace, cyberattacks, disinformation campaigns and sabotage. Foreign Minister Dan Neculaescu said the fire in Brasov was “part of a broader campaign of sabotage across Europe” targeting military production. “Hybrid attacks will not hold us back from strengthening our resilience and defense,” he wrote on X. The accusation follows a string of incidents at defence sites across Europe in recent weeks. In September, explosions and a fire erupted at an ammunition storage site in Bulgaria, weeks after a blaze at another munitions facility in the country. Both sites are operated by the Bulgarian arms maker EMCO, whose munitions are used in Ukraine. That same month, firebombs were thrown near the offices of a defence company in Munich, and Romanian authorities said they had detained a Russian citizen accused of filming and photographing military sites in preparation for sabotage. In August, a blast struck an ammunition factory near Rome in Italy operated by the arms maker KNDS. At sea, at least eight cargo ships have been hit off the coasts of Romania and Bulgaria over the past three weeks, and about 34 sailors have been reported dead or missing. Dan, the Romanian president, has called the attacks on ships in Romanian waters “a new example of the tragic consequences of Russia’s aggression against Ukraine”. A year ago, Poland and Romania also detained eight people suspected of taking part in a Russian plot to send exploding parcels to Ukraine.
